3	\subsection{Event Extraction Validation}
4	\label{sec:wikievents}
5	
6	Zero-shot evaluation on WikiEvents (246 documents, 3 models; Appendices~\ref{app:wikievents-pilot},~\ref{app:wikievents},~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}) confirms constraint applicability to event extraction, with EV and RoV violations eliminated across all models; fine-tuning composability is preliminary ($n{=}20$).

3	\section{Introduction}
4	\label{sec:introduction}
5	
6	Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
7	We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
8	Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
9	At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.
10	
11	Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
12	Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
13	Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
14	Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
15	Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.
16	
17	We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
18	A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
19	OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
20	LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency).
21	DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations (DR+CF) decreasing 30--51\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
22	
23	OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.
24	
25	Our contributions:

27	    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only constraints reduce domain-range violations by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, but their composition achieves 94\%---revealing an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations (DR+CF) decreasing 30--51\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only constraints reduce domain-range violations by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, but their composition achieves 94\%---revealing an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework showing that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Evidence of scale-dependent layer interaction on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4): the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%---the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.
On DocRED (96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), grammar-only \emph{increases} DR via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: forcing OOV$\to$valid relation mapping exposes violations previously masked by vocabulary errors (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:docred-zs-ablation}).
Cross-model validation (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}) confirms DR drops of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings; post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 15--74\% rejection rates.

% === Limitations (ARR requirement: standalone section, does not count toward page limit) ===

\section*{Limitations}

\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
CF is an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement: CF$\leftrightarrow$DR represents a fundamental trade-off (eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}), and its impact is model-dependent (S1 introduces CF for calibrated models but reduces it for poorly-calibrated ones).
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF.
Entity-first generation order is an architectural constraint: the grammar enforces entities before relations, ensuring the registry is populated before type checks; alternative orderings would require deferred constraint evaluation.
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations total) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors (28\%); schema gaps arise from training-data-derived constraints that may not cover all valid type pairs (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
Our empirical constraints are derived from training data type-pair co-occurrences; schema evolution (adding new entity types or relations) would require constraint regeneration, and the 0.6--1.0\% uncovered valid type pairs suggest potential over-restriction during transition periods.
We do not decompose CF violations into first-seen cascading errors versus legitimate type ambiguity; this decomposition requires gold entity type annotations at the mention level, which SciERC provides only at the entity level.
Post-hoc type consensus re-voting eliminates all CF in our experiments, at the cost of DR regression (up to $+$9.38\,pp on DocRED zero-shot; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}); integrating consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated on two 8B-class models (full datasets) and one 70B-class model (SciERC full, DocRED 200-document subset).
Scaling to smaller models has not been verified; the schema restrictiveness--enforcement difficulty relationship is based on three schemas.
Evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); LoRA hyperparameters were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization, which may underestimate DocRED potential.
WikiEvents fine-tuning is preliminary ($n{=}20$); DocRED uses the development set (test annotations unavailable).
All main experiments use greedy decoding; beam search compatibility is confirmed but comprehensive evaluation across all configurations remains future work (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}).
Composability with training-based schema-aware systems (e.g., GoLLIE) is architecturally supported but not empirically validated in this work.

\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
Our approach requires access to model logits, excluding API-only models; continuation masking assumes distinguishable token prefixes per type name, which may be challenged by morphologically similar types (e.g., \texttt{Protein} vs.\ \texttt{Protein\_Complex}; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
70B experiments use AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms enforcement is unaffected (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}), though a direct 70B FP16 comparison exceeds our hardware capacity.
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets; the mechanism is language-independent but CJK tokenization fragmentation may increase masking steps (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
While composability is validated with both LoRA and full fine-tuning (Appendix~\ref{app:full-ft}), different PEFT methods may affect logit distributions differently, and further validation across adapter methods is warranted.
The two-pass strategy (S2) exhibits scale-dependent degradation: at 70B, S2 reduces R-F1 by 8.45\,pp while 8B models show comparable S1/S2 performance, suggesting optimal constraint granularity varies with model capacity (Appendix~\ref{app:70b-ablation}).

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available benchmark datasets (SciERC, DocRED, and WikiEvents) with no personally identifiable information.
No human subjects were involved in the experiments.

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

2	
3	We validated OntoCoDec across 2 RE datasets, 3 model families, and event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
4	The central finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
5	
6	\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
7	This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
8	We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
9	Fallback frequency varies dramatically across architectures (0 vs.\ 5{,}882 under LoRA+S1) without affecting enforcement (both DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%), confirming grammar is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve.
10	Constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
11	
12	\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
13	Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
14	Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
15	Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
16	Net effect: total violations (DR+CF) decrease 30--51\% in zero-shot and 26--52\% under fine-tuned greedy S1; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all. DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
17	
18	\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Fallback frequency varies dramatically across architectures (0 vs.\ 5{,}882 under LoRA+S1) without affecting enforcement (both DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%), confirming grammar is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve.
Constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations (DR+CF) decrease 30--51\% in zero-shot and 26--52\% under fine-tuned greedy S1; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all. DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%).
S2 (two-pass) degrades at 70B ($-$8\,pp R-F1), consistent with CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane}; we recommend S1 as default.

The root cause---per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability})---requires global entity-level consensus beyond online masking; beam search and TCR approximate this, with full integration as future work.
